title: Z-K-R
hookLine: zachor, zikaron: memory as something you do

lines: A WIND, AND THE WATERS GO DOWN.
cards: "And God remembered Noah." The water still covers everything. The ark is drifting.

Nothing in the story has moved for a long time. Then comes that sentence, and right after it, God sends a wind across the earth, and the waters begin to go down. Remembering here isn't a thought drifting through a mind.
It's the hinge, the moment things start to move again. Today's root is memory that does something.

teach.b: Z-K-R. Zayin, kaf, resh. Four places it shows up.
First, when God remembers. Noah is one. In Exodus, the people groan under slavery, and "God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob."
A few verses on, Moses is standing at a burning bush. Memory, again, is where rescue starts. Second, zachor, remember, as a command.
"Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." It isn't asking anyone to recall that the Sabbath exists. Remembering it means keeping it: lighting candles, setting a table, a day set apart.
Third, zikaron, a memorial. Of the Passover night, the Torah says: "And this day shall be unto you for a memorial."
The seder is remembering done with hands and mouth: matzah to chew, bitter herbs to taste, questions asked out loud. Fourth, people.

teach.h: MAY THEIR MEMORY BE A BLESSING.
teach.b: When a Jew mentions someone who has died, it's customary to add zichrono livracha, may his memory be a blessing.
The memory is given a job. And since today ends a week, look back at its roots. K-D-Sh, set apart.
Tz-D-K, giving as justice. Ch-S-D, kindness. A-M-N, steadiness.
Emet, truth with its first letter. Sh-M-A, hearing that heeds. And now Z-K-R.
Read closely, each one turns out to be a thing you do.

how: Jews remember through acts: keeping the Sabbath, eating the foods of the Passover seder, lighting a memorial candle on the anniversary of a death, and adding 'may their memory be a blessing' after a name.

o: a root that means to write something down
remembering that leads to doing something
a root that means to forget and let go

games.q: you're in Egypt, groaning under slavery. the text says God heard, and remembered the covenant. what comes next in the story?
o: nothing changes for a long while.
Moses meets God at a burning bush.
games.why: a few verses after "God remembered his covenant," Moses is at the burning bush. in this root, memory is where rescue begins.

practice: Bring to mind one person who isn't in your life the way they once were, someone who has died or someone far away, and say their name quietly.
Then say one thing they did, with their hands or their words, not a feeling about them, and let it sit for a few breaths.
If the person has died, you can add zichrono livracha, or zichronah livracha for a woman: may their memory be a blessing.
